prompt: What does a pipeline add to the SQL Ana ran by hand in `warehouse-modeling`?
hint: The work is the same; the difference is who is watching.

choices.text: Repetition with nobody watching
choices.why: Right. Moving and transforming data was already there; repetition without a person is what is new.

choices.text: Transforming the data on the way
choices.why: The hand-run SQL already transformed the data. That is not what changes.

choices.text: A faster database engine for the warehouse
choices.why: The engine is not the subject. The same warehouse is filled either way.

choices.text: Moving data from the shop to the warehouse
choices.why: Ana's commands moved the data too. A one-off copy is not a pipeline.

prompt: Why does the course have you write extraction, transformation and loading by hand before Airflow appears?
hint: Think about what a scheduler is given.

choices.text: Because Airflow does not run Python, so the steps have to exist elsewhere first
choices.why: It runs Python; its DAGs are written in it.

choices.text: A scheduler runs what it is given, and a bad step stays bad
choices.why: Right. The tool adds timing and retries, not correctness.

choices.text: Because the lab installs Airflow only in lesson 8
choices.why: The lab installs everything on the first run of `setup.sh`.

choices.text: Because hand-written steps run faster than the same steps run by a scheduler
choices.why: Speed is not the argument; the same code runs either way.

prompt: Why does the lab give Airflow, dbt, Prefect and Dagster one virtual environment each?
hint: What would happen if they shared one?

choices.text: To save disk space
choices.why: Separate environments take more disk, not less.

choices.text: They pin conflicting versions of the same libraries
choices.why: Right. One environment per tool keeps each one's pins intact.

choices.text: So that each tool runs as a different Linux user
choices.why: Everything runs as `ana`; the environments are about libraries.

choices.text: Because the tools need different Python interpreters to run
choices.why: All of them run on the same Python 3.13 here.

prompt: The lab's data takes 19 MB and its software 1.3 GB. About how many times larger is the software than the data? Give a whole number.
hint: 1.3 GB is about 1,300 MB.

prompt: `setup.sh` stopped with an error. Which line should you read first?
hint: The script stops at the first error.

choices.text: The first line it printed
choices.why: The start of the run is what worked. The script stops at the failure.

choices.text: The last line it printed
choices.why: Right. It stops at the first error, so the last line is the one that broke.

choices.text: The PostgreSQL server log
choices.why: That helps only when the database is the problem. Start with what the script said.

choices.text: Whatever `pip` printed, since pip fails most
choices.why: Pip is one of four failures; the last line tells you which.

prompt: A pipeline's output disagrees with the lesson's numbers after you corrected a row of the shop by hand. What do you do?
hint: The lab has one way back to a known state.

choices.text: Run `sudo shop reset` and play the days again
choices.why: Right. Reset returns the shop to 28 February, so the numbers match again.

choices.text: Edit the warehouse tables until the totals match the lesson's
choices.why: That hides the difference instead of removing its cause.

choices.text: Undo the edit with another `UPDATE` that puts the old value back
choices.why: The pipelines may already have read the edited row; a second edit does not undo that.

choices.text: Rebuild the lab with `setup.sh`
choices.why: `up` skips what is already built and leaves the shop as it is.

prompt: What does `shop day 2026-03-01` do to the shop's database?
hint: It is a day of trade, not a pile of rows.

choices.text: Inserts that day's orders and nothing else
choices.why: It also updates customers and old orders, and some days it deletes a customer.

choices.text: Replays that day's inserts, updates and deletes, in order
choices.why: Right. The tills, the website and the back office, as they ran.

choices.text: Replaces the database with a copy taken at the end of that day
choices.why: Nothing is replaced; the day's statements run against the database as it stands.

choices.text: Moves the system clock forward one day
choices.why: The machine's clock is untouched; the shop's data moves forward.

prompt: On 1 March, four customers moved city and five old orders were refunded or cancelled. Why does that matter more to a pipeline than the 183 new orders?
hint: Think of a copy taken on 28 February.

choices.text: Updates are slower to read from the shop than inserts
choices.why: Speed is not the issue; finding them is.

choices.text: They make rows a copy already holds wrong
choices.why: Right. New rows are easy to find; changed old rows are what lessons 4 and 5 are about.

choices.text: Refunded orders are deleted from the shop
choices.why: A refund is an `UPDATE` of the status; the order stays.

choices.text: The warehouse refuses updates
choices.why: The warehouse accepts whatever the pipeline writes.

prompt: To return the shop to the night of 28 February, you run `sudo shop ___`.
hint: The clock only goes forward; this is the way back.

prompt: Which of these does a pipeline need that a script run once by hand did not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Imagine nobody is watching it.

choices.text: Knowing which rows it already copied
choices.why: Yes. Otherwise tonight repeats yesterday or skips what arrived during it.

choices.text: Giving the same result when run twice
choices.why: Yes. A rerun after a failure must not double the data.

choices.text: Saying when it fails, and where
choices.why: Yes. A silent failure leaves yesterday's numbers on the screen.

choices.text: Being written in SQL rather than Python
choices.why: Either language serves; the course uses both.

prompt: A pipeline inserts the day's rows into the report table one at a time over ten minutes. A manager opens the report during those minutes. What do they see?
hint: The destination is the half people forget.

choices.text: An error, because the table is locked
choices.why: Inserts do not stop readers in PostgreSQL; they see what is committed.

choices.text: Yesterday's complete numbers, until the load ends
choices.why: That is what a load into a separate table that is swapped at the end gives.

choices.text: Part of the day, which looks like a complete one
choices.why: Right. Nothing on the screen says the day is half loaded.

choices.text: Nothing at all until the pipeline finishes
choices.why: Rows committed one at a time are visible one at a time.

prompt: Ana's report is fed by a nightly batch that runs at 2 a.m. and loads the day before. Someone opens it at 4 p.m. on 2 March. What is the latest day it can show?
hint: The run loads a period that has already closed.

choices.text: 2 March, up to 2 a.m.
choices.why: The run loads whole days, and 2 March has not closed yet.

choices.text: 2 March, up to 4 p.m.
choices.why: That would need a run after 4 p.m. that loads part of today.

choices.text: 28 February
choices.why: The 2 a.m. run on 2 March loaded 1 March.

choices.text: 1 March
choices.why: Right. A day that ended sixteen hours before the report was opened.

prompt: Why does `batch.py` take the day as an argument instead of working out yesterday from the clock?
hint: Think about rerunning a failed night.

choices.text: So it loads whichever day it is given, even a failed one
choices.why: Right. A script that decides the day itself loads one day and no other.

choices.text: Because Python has no way to read the clock
choices.why: It has; `datetime.date.today()` reads it.

choices.text: Because the orders in the shop's database carry no timestamps
choices.why: Every order has `ordered_at`; the query filters on it.

choices.text: To make the run faster
choices.why: The argument changes which day is read, not how fast.

prompt: After `batch.py 2026-03-01` ran twice, how many rows did `daily_sales` hold?
hint: Seven shops, twice.

prompt: Why does `consume.py` write its offset after handling an event and not before?
hint: Think about a crash between the two steps.

choices.text: Writing it before would be slower
choices.why: The cost is the same; the order decides what a crash loses.

choices.text: A crash in between then reads one event twice instead of skipping one
choices.why: Right. Twice can be made harmless; skipped is a hole nobody sees.

choices.text: The file is not readable until the offset is written
choices.why: The offset file is the consumer's own; the events file is unaffected.

choices.text: The replay waits for the offset before writing more
choices.why: The writer knows nothing about the reader.

prompt: The second run of `consume.py` began at byte 19764 and its first window was 3.5 seconds behind. Why that much?
hint: Something happened while nothing was reading.

choices.text: The consumer reread the first run's events
choices.why: It started at the saved offset, after them.

choices.text: The website slowed down
choices.why: The replay kept its pace; the reader was the one stopped.

choices.text: Events kept arriving during the three-second pause and were read late
choices.why: Right. They were caught up in one go, then the lag fell back to about a second.

choices.text: Starting Python takes three seconds
choices.why: The first run started just as fast and showed under two.

prompt: Match each kind of ingestion to what it can honestly say about its data.
hint: One closes a period; the other never closes.

pairs.right: Everything up to the last event I saw
The last five minutes are loaded

right_distractors: Every event, in the order it happened

prompt: Ponto Final wants a screen that says whether a book is in stock right now. What does the lesson recommend?
hint: Who already knows the answer exactly?

choices.text: A micro-batch every minute into the warehouse
choices.why: Still up to a minute wrong, about something the source knows now.

choices.text: Asking the source system, with no pipeline
choices.why: Right. A copy a second old is only a second wrong about what the till could say exactly.

choices.text: The nightly batch
choices.why: An answer up to a day old cannot say what is in stock now.

choices.text: A lambda architecture with two paths
choices.why: Two paths double the logic without making it more current than the source.

prompt: What is the cost a kappa architecture accepts in exchange for not writing its logic twice?
hint: History has to come from somewhere.

choices.text: Keeping every event in a log long enough to read it again
choices.why: Right. Replaying the log is how it rebuilds history.

choices.text: Answers a day old
choices.why: That is batch; kappa streams.

choices.text: Two systems that must agree
choices.why: That is lambda's cost, the one kappa avoids.

choices.text: Losing late events
choices.why: Replaying the log reads late events too.

prompt: Order these questions from the one whose answer may be oldest to the one that must be most current.
hint: Put an age on each one.
items: Is this book in stock now
trap: A morning's sales can wait an hour; stock asked at the till cannot wait at all.

prompt: A streaming consumer saves its offset BEFORE handling each event. It crashes once, mid-event. What is wrong afterwards, and how would anyone notice?
hint: The offset says the event was handled.

choices.text: One event is counted twice, visible as a duplicate id
choices.why: That is what saving AFTER risks.

choices.text: The consumer refuses to start again
choices.why: It starts happily, from the saved offset.

choices.text: Nothing, because the replay writes the event again
choices.why: The writer does not know the reader crashed.

choices.text: One event is lost, and nothing shows it
choices.why: Right. The restart begins after it, and a missing event leaves no trace to find.
